section.title: A Good Servant of Christ Jesus
section.sectionRationale: Paul warns that in later times some will abandon the faith, following deceiving spirits, forbidding marriage and certain foods, though everything God made is good. Over against this, Timothy is to be a good servant of Christ Jesus: nourished on sound teaching, trained for godliness, an example to believers, watching his life and doctrine closely so as to save himself and his hearers.
section.thesis: Faithful ministry means rejecting ascetic error, receiving God's good gifts with thanksgiving, and training oneself for godliness, so that a young servant of Christ, by watching his life and teaching, is used to save both himself and those who hear him.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the warning against apostasy and asceticism; the call to train for godliness rather than mere physical discipline; and the charge to Timothy to set an example and watch his life and doctrine.

verses.text: Now the Spirit expressly states that in later times some will {{aphistemi|abandon the faith}} to follow deceitful spirits and the teachings of demons,
influenced by the hypocrisy of liars, whose consciences are seared with a hot iron.
They will prohibit marriage and require abstinence from certain foods that God has created to be received with thanksgiving by those who believe and know the truth.
For every {{ktisma|creation}} of God is good, and nothing that is received with thanksgiving should be rejected,
because it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer.

units.label: Train yourself for godliness
units.note: value for this life and the next

verses.text: By pointing out these things to the brothers, you will be a good servant of Christ Jesus, nourished by the words of faith and sound instruction that you have followed.
But reject irreverent, silly myths. Instead, {{gymnazo|train}} yourself for godliness.
For physical exercise is of limited value, but {{eusebeia|godliness}} is valuable in every way, holding promise for the present life and for the one to come.
This is a trustworthy saying, worthy of full acceptance.
To this end we labor and strive, because we have set our hope on the living God, who is the Savior of everyone, and especially of those who believe.

units.label: Watch your life and doctrine
units.note: set an example, do not neglect the gift

verses.text: Let no one despise your youth, but set an {{typos|example}} for the believers in speech, in conduct, in love, in faith, in purity.
Until I come, devote yourself to the public reading of Scripture, to exhortation, and to teaching.
Do not neglect the {{charisma|gift}} that is in you, which was given you through the prophecy spoken over you at the laying on of the hands of the elders.
Be diligent in these matters and absorbed in them, so that your progress will be evident to all.
Pay close attention to your life and to your teaching. Persevere in these things, for by so doing you will save both yourself and those who hear you.

aphistemi.gloss: To stand off, withdraw, or fall away; the root behind our word apostasy. The Spirit warns that some will fall away from the faith they once professed, drawn by deceiving spirits. It names a real departure, not a stumble, and sets the danger this chapter guards against.

ktisma.gloss: A created thing, a creature. Paul affirms every ktisma of God is good, echoing Genesis where God saw all He made as good. This directly refutes the ascetics who forbid marriage and foods, treating parts of God's creation as evil rather than gifts to be received with thanks.

gymnazo.gloss: To train or exercise, as an athlete in the gymnasium; the root of our word gymnasium. Timothy is to train himself for godliness with the discipline an athlete gives his body, showing that growth in godliness is deliberate, strenuous, and habitual, not passive.

eusebeia.gloss: Godliness, reverence for God lived out in daily life, a signature word of the Pastoral Epistles. Paul says it holds value for both the present life and the one to come, far surpassing the limited value of mere physical training. Godliness is the goal of all Timothy's discipline.

typos.gloss: A type, pattern, or example, an impression left that others copy. Despite his youth, Timothy is to be a typos for believers in speech, conduct, love, faith, and purity. A leader teaches not only by words but by a life others can safely imitate.

charisma.gloss: A gift of grace, an ability given by God for service. Timothy received his through prophecy and the laying on of the elders' hands. Paul warns him not to neglect it but to stir it into use, for gifts unexercised grow cold.

basic.context: The Spirit warns that some will fall away from the faith, misled by demonic teaching that forbids marriage and certain foods. Paul answers that everything God made is good and is to be received with thanksgiving. Timothy is to be a good servant of Christ Jesus, feeding on sound teaching and training himself for godliness, which is valuable for this life and the next. Though young, he is to set an example and watch his life and doctrine closely.
basic.hermeneutics: The warning about later times applies to the church's whole age, not one distant moment. The refutation of asceticism is prescriptive: God's good gifts are to be enjoyed with thanks, not treated as evil. The charge to Timothy models what every servant of Christ is to pursue, godliness, example, and perseverance in life and teaching.
basic.originalLanguages: Some will aphistemi, fall away, from the faith. Yet every ktisma, creation, of God is good. Timothy must gymnazo, train, himself for eusebeia, godliness, valuable now and forever. He is to be a typos, example, to believers and not neglect the charisma, gift, given to him.
basic.typology: The good creation received with thanksgiving looks back to Eden, where God pronounced all things good, and forward to the redeemed enjoyment of all things in the new creation. Timothy the young example prefigures the many leaders Christ raises to shepherd His people.
basic.christ: Timothy is to be a good servant of Christ Jesus, and the hope of the labor is set on the living God, the Savior of all. The ministry of reading, exhortation, and teaching centers on the words of faith, the gospel of Christ, by which people are saved.
basic.god: God is the living God who made all things good and is the Savior of everyone, especially those who believe. He gives good gifts to be received with thanksgiving, sanctified by His word and prayer. He is not a God who despises His creation but one who fills it with grace.
basic.crossReferences: Genesis 1 declares all God made very good. First Corinthians 10 says receive food with thanksgiving to God. Second Timothy 1 urges Timothy to fan into flame the gift of God.
basic.oneStory: God made a good world, and error has always tried either to indulge it wrongly or to reject it as evil. Here God defends His good gifts and raises up faithful servants trained for godliness. It is part of His long work of forming a people who receive His grace with thanks and hold fast the gospel through every generation.

context.literary:
The chapter is built as a hinge. Verses 1 to 5 are a forecast about others, verses 6 to 16 are a charge to Timothy, and the first word of the charge, 'By pointing out these things,' in verse 6, ties the two halves together: the way to serve well is to name the error plainly and then to be a different kind of person. Inside the charge the movement is almost a training programme. Verse 7 gives the rejection and the discipline in a single breath, verse 8 gives the reason, verses 9 and 10 give a sealed saying and the goal that drives it, verse 11 turns to command, and verses 12 to 16 pile up imperatives: set an example, devote yourself, do not neglect, be diligent, pay close attention, persevere.

The trustworthy saying of verse 9 is one of five in the letters to Timothy and Titus, and its placement is a puzzle. It stands either after verse 8, summing up the value of godliness, or before verse 10, introducing the labour and hope. The wording of verse 10 begins 'To this end,' which points back to the whole thought of godliness and hope, so the saying probably underlines both.

The list in verse 12, speech, conduct, love, faith, purity, covers the whole person, outside to inside. Verses 13 to 15 name three public duties, reading, exhortation and teaching, and then a gift, and the verbs get more intense as they go, from 'devote yourself' to 'be absorbed.' The closing verse folds everything into two objects, 'your life' and 'your teaching,' and says the two must be held together. A watched life with careless teaching, or sound teaching with a careless life, fails the test. The chapter ends where the false teachers began, in the realm of teaching and conduct, so that the contrast between them and Timothy is complete.
context.historical:
Timothy was probably in his thirties, young by the standard of the ancient world, where the word for a young man could stretch to forty. Elders in a Greek or Jewish town were respected for age, and a younger delegate of an apostle faced the real risk of being brushed aside. Paul's answer is not to lower Timothy's authority but to anchor it in his example and in the gift given him.

The errors Paul names, forbidding marriage and certain foods, belong to a stream of religious thought, found in Jewish and Greek circles, that prized bodily denial as a path to purity. Colossians 2:16 to 23 describes a related teaching in the nearby Lycus valley, with rules about food and drink and a show of humility and severe treatment of the body. Paul does not name the group at Ephesus, and it is safer to describe the pattern than to attach a modern label to it. His reply shows he regarded it as a distortion of the Jewish law and of creation itself.

The public reading of Scripture in verse 13 reflects the synagogue practice that the first churches inherited, in which the Law and the Prophets were read aloud and then explained, as in Acts 13:15 and Luke 4:16 to 21. Most believers could not read or own scrolls, so hearing the word read was the chief way they met it. To this Paul adds exhortation and teaching, the application and explanation that follow the reading. The laying on of hands in verse 14 echoes the way Israel set people apart, as with Joshua in Numbers 27:18 to 23, and here it is joined with a prophetic word and the presence of the elders, the council of the local church.
context.canonical:
The goodness of creation that Paul defends runs through the whole Bible. Genesis 1 repeats that what God made was good, and Genesis 9:3 gives Noah every moving thing as food after the flood. The Law divided clean from unclean for Israel, but Jesus declared all foods clean, Mark 7:19, Peter was told in a vision not to call common what God has made clean, Acts 10:15, and Paul writes in Romans 14:14 that nothing is unclean in itself. In 1 Corinthians 10:25 to 31 he tells believers to eat what is sold in the market and to do everything to the glory of God. First Timothy 4 gathers these strands into one sentence.

On marriage, Genesis 2:18 to 24 shows it as God's gift before the fall, and Hebrews 13:4 says it should be honoured by all. Yet Paul himself, in 1 Corinthians 7:7 and 7:32 to 35, commends singleness as a gift for those called to it. The two fit together because the error is not in choosing the single life but in forbidding marriage as though it were defiling.

The charge to Timothy to guard his gift has its closest parallel in 2 Timothy 1:6 and 1:13 to 14, and the picture of the athlete returns in 2 Timothy 2:5 and 4:7. The word 'godliness' and the call to be an example are echoed in Titus 2:7. First Peter 5:3 uses the same word for an example when it tells elders to be examples to the flock, not lords over it.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul wanted Timothy to be able to name the false teaching, to answer it from creation and from the word of God, and to stay steady when others looked down on his youth. The warning is meant to steady the church, not frighten it. 'Later times' means the whole span between the first and second comings, so Timothy is not told to wait for a distant villain but to expect these voices in his own city and to recognise them by what they forbid.

The core of the answer is a doctrine of thanks. Food and marriage are received, and the receiving is done with thanksgiving, blessed by the word of God and by prayer. A person who gives thanks cannot treat a gift as a stain. Paul then redirects the energy of the ascetics toward what actually matters. He does not tell Timothy to stop training; he tells him to train for godliness rather than for a clean outward show. The charge to Timothy, to read, teach, and watch his life, is the practical form of the same conviction, that the church is held up by sound words and by a life that matches them.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The prophecy of verses 1 to 3 describes what the Spirit says will happen. It does not tell the church to expect defeat. What is prescribed is the response: reject the myths, receive the gifts, train for godliness, set an example, and attend to the public reading of Scripture. Some details are tied to Timothy's situation. The laying on of hands and the particular prophecy were part of his own commissioning, and Paul's words 'Until I come' fit his own absence. They are not a rule that every church must repeat the same ceremony or wait for an apostle.

The passage does not forbid every discipline. Fasting, simplicity, and singleness have their place elsewhere in Scripture. What it forbids is treating them as mandatory marks of holiness or as proof that created things are evil. A believer today applies it by asking two questions of any restriction: does it flow from thanks and freedom, or does it declare God's gifts unclean? And does it lead to godliness, or only to a look of seriousness?

debates.question: In what sense is God 'the Savior of everyone, and especially of those who believe' in verse 10?

views.label: Saviour as preserver of all, and of believers eternally
views.case: The word 'savior' can describe a rescuer from danger, and God gives life, breath and daily good to all, as Paul says to the Athenians in Acts 17:25 and Jesus says of the sun and rain in Matthew 5:45. Eternal salvation is for those who believe. 'Especially' separates two groups in a single class of benefit, the believers receiving the fullest form of it.

views.label: Christ's death offered to all, applied to believers
views.case: Paul says in 1 Timothy 2:6 that Christ gave Himself as a ransom for all, and in 2:4 that God wants all to be saved. On this view the atonement is sufficient for the world and the gospel is sincerely offered to everyone, but its saving effect belongs to those who trust Him. 'Especially' marks the believers as those who actually receive what is offered.

views.label: All kinds of people, with believers the actual saved
views.case: Many in the Reformed tradition read 'all' in these letters as people of every rank and nation, as 2:1 to 2 suggests with its prayer for kings and all in authority. God is Saviour of people from every group, and in the fullest sense of those who believe.

debates.bearing: None of the three reads this as teaching that everyone is saved regardless of faith, since the clause 'those who believe' is the very thing that marks the saved. All of them hold that God's kindness reaches beyond the church, which is why Paul can say the labour of ministry is worth the toil.

debates.question: What does Paul mean that Timothy will 'save both yourself and those who hear you' in verse 16?

views.label: Perseverance as the path along which God keeps His own
views.case: Salvation is by grace through faith, but Scripture also warns that those who do not hold on are in danger, as in 4:1 itself. By watching his life and teaching, Timothy remains in the faith, and his hearers are rescued by the same gospel.

views.label: Ministry as God's means of saving others
views.case: God ordinarily saves through the preached word, Romans 10:14 to 17. Timothy does not rescue anyone by his own power; he is the instrument God uses, and his faithfulness is part of how his hearers come to faith.

debates.bearing: Both views refuse to make Timothy a saviour. They keep faithful ministry bound to God's grace, and they insist that careless teaching or a careless life can cost real people dearly.

debates.question: What is the 'later times' of verse 1?

views.label: The whole age between the comings
views.case: The New Testament often treats the whole age as the last days, Acts 2:17 and Hebrews 1:2. Paul uses the present tense in the next chapter, 'the Spirit expressly states,' and tells Timothy to deal with the error now, which suggests it is already at work.

views.label: A particular season of intensified apostasy
views.case: Some read the phrase together with 2 Timothy 3:1 and 2 Thessalonians 2:3 as a more intense period close to the end, when departure from the faith grows.

debates.bearing: Either way, Timothy is to act now. The church is never told to wait for a final time to watch for such teaching.

study.originalLanguages:
The forecast of verse 1 says some will abandon the faith. The verb is aphistemi, to stand away, and it is the root of the later noun apostasia, used for the great rebellion in 2 Thessalonians 2:3. The tense is future, a settled prediction, and the object is 'the faith,' meaning the body of belief, not merely private trust. Paul's phrase for the influences at work, 'deceitful spirits and the teachings of demons,' makes the source spiritual, though the carriers are men, 'liars' in verse 2, who are said to have consciences 'seared with a hot iron.' The verb is a perfect participle, which describes a settled state: a conscience that has been burned until it no longer feels. The picture is of a brand or cautery, a once-sensitive nerve now numb.

In verse 4 the word for 'received,' translated from lambano in the sense of accepting something offered, goes with 'thanksgiving,' eucharistia. The sentence that says every creation of God is good and nothing is to be rejected places thanks as the hinge: what is received with thanks is sanctified, verse 5, by 'the word of God and prayer.' The word for prayer here, enteuxis, is a petition made to God on behalf of someone, used in 1 Timothy 2:1 for the intercessions that begin the letter. The word of God may mean the creation word of Genesis 1, the later word of God declaring foods clean, or the blessing spoken at the table, and the likely sense includes all three.

Verse 7 sets two verbs against each other. The false teachers' myths are to be refused, using the word paraiteomai, to decline or excuse oneself from, which is also used in Hebrews 12:25. The positive command is gymnazo, from which English gets gymnasium, to train naked in the exercise yard. The same verb is used in Hebrews 5:14 of those whose senses are trained and in Hebrews 12:11 of training through discipline. Paul's contrast in verse 8 between 'physical exercise,' gymnasia, and godliness, eusebeia, does not despise the body; it says bodily discipline is 'of limited value,' using a word that can mean 'for a little while' or 'to a small extent.' Godliness is valuable 'in every way,' with a promise for 'the present life and the one to come.'

Verse 10 joins two verbs with a deliberate sting. 'Labor,' kopiao, is the weariness of hard work, and 'strive,' agonizomai, is the same word as the contest of the athlete, so the training is seen as strenuous. Paul uses the same pair in Colossians 1:29. In verse 12 the word typos, an example or pattern, comes from the mark left by a strike, then a mould or model. Paul uses it of himself in Philippians 3:17 and of the elders in 1 Peter 5:3 in the same sense. In verse 15, 'be diligent' translates meletao, which means to ponder, practise or rehearse, and 'absorbed' is literally 'be in these things.' The Septuagint uses the same verb for meditating on the law in Psalm 1:2.

typology.type: Creation received with thanks, from Eden to the new earth
typology.fulfillment: Paul's claim that everything God created is good takes the reader back to Genesis 1:31 and forward to a restored creation. In Eden the man and woman were told to eat freely from every tree but one, Genesis 2:16. In Christ the sentence is renewed: all foods are cleansed, Mark 7:19, and Paul tells the Corinthians that the earth and its fullness belong to the Lord, 1 Corinthians 10:26. The type is limited because creation is still under the curse, Romans 8:20 to 21, and eating with thanks is a foretaste of the feast at the marriage supper of the Lamb, Revelation 19:9.

The runner and wrestler are among Paul's favourite pictures, 1 Corinthians 9:24 to 27 and 2 Timothy 4:7. In Christ the contest changes. The prize is not a perishable crown but an imperishable one, 1 Corinthians 9:25, and the strength is supplied by God, Colossians 1:29, so that the striving is real but never the ground of acceptance. The image falls short if it implies the athlete earns the place. The believer trains because the race has already been won in Christ, who 'endured the cross' and sits at God's right hand, Hebrews 12:2.

typology.type: Timothy as an example, and the laying on of hands
typology.fulfillment: Israel set leaders apart by laying on hands, as with Joshua, who was filled with the spirit of wisdom, Deuteronomy 34:9. Timothy's commissioning follows that pattern, and his role as a model recalls the way Moses and Joshua and the prophets were set before Israel to be imitated. In Christ the pattern reaches its centre. Jesus washed His disciples' feet and said He had given them an example, John 13:15, and Paul says to imitate him as he imitates Christ, 1 Corinthians 11:1. The example of any minister is derivative, a reflection of the one Shepherd, and fails whenever it points to itself.

study.christ:
Verse 6 names Timothy a good servant of Christ Jesus, and the entire chapter is written so that the title is true. The Greek word for servant, diakonos, belongs to the same family as the verb Jesus uses of Himself in Mark 10:45, where He says He did not come to be served but to serve and to give His life as a ransom. The good servant of Christ is therefore a servant of One who Himself served, and every part of Timothy's training is a following of that shape.

The chapter leads to Christ by the confession of verse 10. The living God is the Saviour of all people, and especially of believers, and the gospel's centre is a Person: the letter earlier says Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, 1 Timothy 1:15, and that there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, 2:5. The hope that drives the labour is not a hope in the minister's own effort but in the God whom Christ makes known.

It also leads to Christ by contrast with the false teachers. They forbid what God made and call it holiness. Jesus, who was called a glutton and a drunkard by His critics, Matthew 11:19, ate with tax collectors, and went to the wedding at Cana, John 2:1 to 11, where He made wine. He declared all foods clean, Mark 7:19. His first sign was at a marriage feast, and He used a wedding as the picture of the kingdom, Matthew 22:2. The true Master does not despise the creation He made, and He does not require His servants to despise it.

The call to be an example places the pattern in Christ's own life. Jesus said He had set an example, John 13:15, and Paul says Christ left an example for us to follow in His steps, 1 Peter 2:21. Timothy's life is therefore meant to be a readable copy of Christ's, in speech, conduct, love, faith and purity. The pairing 'your life and your teaching' is the shape of Jesus' own ministry, which Luke summarises as 'all that Jesus began to do and to teach,' Acts 1:1.

A caution is in order. It would stretch the text to find Christ in each detail of the gift or the laying on of hands. The links rest on the apostle's own words, and the point is the same one the letter keeps making: the gospel is a person to be known, a body of teaching to be guarded, and a way of life to be followed, and all three are Christ's.
study.god:
The chapter shows God first as Creator who does not repent of His gifts. Everything He made is good, and the goodness is not cancelled by the fall, because it can still be received with thanks. To deny this is to accuse the Maker. The false teachers think they are more spiritual than God, who made bodies, bread and marriage, and said it was good.

It shows God as the living God, a phrase that sets Him against the dead myths of verse 7 and the lifeless regulations of verse 3. A living God is the one who speaks, so the word of God sanctifies, and who hears, so prayer sanctifies. Timothy's hope rests in that God, who is not a figure of speech or a principle but one who acts.

It shows God as Saviour of everyone in a real sense and of believers in the fullest. Whatever view of the grammar is taken, the sentence says God's care is wider than the church while His saving purpose is concentrated on those who trust Him. This holds together two things people often split: His generosity to all and His particular grace to His own. It is the reason a minister may labour for anyone, and the reason the labour does not go unrewarded.

God appears as the giver of gifts to His servants. The gift in Timothy was given through prophecy with the laying on of hands, which means it came from God, and Paul can tell him not to neglect it precisely because it is not his own achievement. God supplies, and the servant stirs the gift into use.

God is also one who holds the servant accountable for the shape of his work. Timothy is to watch his life and his teaching because both are noticed. The promise of verse 8, 'for the present life and for the one to come,' says that God is not a God of this world only or of the next only. He cares about daily conduct and about the final end.

For worship, the chapter calls for thanksgiving at the table and at the marriage bed, and for steady labour at godliness. A believer who eats with gratitude and trains with hope worships in the same act. Prayer before a meal is not decoration; it is, as Paul says, part of what makes the meal holy.

crossReferences.note: After the sixth day God looked at everything He had made, and it was very good. Paul's claim in verse 4 that every creation of God is good stands on this verdict. No later fall or law can undo what God declared at the start about the material world.

After the flood God gave Noah every moving thing as food, as He had given the green plants. The permission pre-dates the law of Moses, so the later food laws were a particular provision for Israel and not a universal rule about the purity of creatures.

Jesus declared all foods clean when He said that what enters a person goes into the stomach and not the heart. Paul's answer to the ascetics of Ephesus is the same teaching applied to a church that was tempted to treat abstinence as holiness.

The voice told Peter not to call common what God has made clean. The lesson began with food and moved at once to people, showing that the cleansing of creation reaches the Gentiles too. Paul's argument is of the same family.

Paul says nothing is unclean in itself, but it is unclean to the one who regards it so. The sentence helps in applying 1 Timothy 4: a weak conscience is to be treated gently, though the false teachers go further and make the rule mandatory.

If I take part in a meal with thanks, Paul asks, why should I be denounced over something for which I give thanks? The question is almost the argument of 1 Timothy 4:4 to 5, that a meal received with thanksgiving is blessed.

Paul says every athlete exercises self control to win a perishable crown, but we an imperishable. The image of the contest that stands behind 'train yourself' gives the aim, and shows that discipline is real, and aims at lasting reward.

Paul tells Timothy to fan into flame the gift of God that is in him through the laying on of Paul's hands. The command is nearly the same as 1 Timothy 4:14, and both stress that a gift needs to be stirred up, not left idle.

Paul tells Titus to show himself in all respects a pattern of good works, with integrity and dignity in teaching. The instruction is the twin of 1 Timothy 4:12 and shows that example and doctrine belong together for every young minister.

Peter tells elders not to lord it over those entrusted to them but to be examples to the flock. The word for 'example' is the same as in 1 Timothy 4:12, and the passage shows that Paul's request to Timothy was a general principle of leadership.

Paul says that rules of self-made worship and severe treatment of the body have an appearance of wisdom but no value against the indulgence of the flesh. This is a close parallel to 1 Timothy 4:8, where bodily discipline is of limited value.

study.oneStory:
Genesis begins with a creation that God calls good and with a command to eat freely, Genesis 1:31 and 2:16. The fall introduced a world in which the good things of creation could be misused, and humanity has since swung between two errors: worshipping the gifts and despising them. Paul meets the second error here. Asceticism that treats the material world as evil is not a higher holiness but a quiet slander of the Maker, and the church is called to keep the original verdict.

The passage also answers a question the Old Testament leaves open: how will the people of God relate to the nations and their foods, their tables and their marriages? The Law drew lines for Israel, but through Christ the wall has been taken down, Ephesians 2:14, and a church of Jews and Gentiles can sit at one table. First Timothy 4:3 to 5 is the ordinary working of that, a plain claim that thanks and the word of God make a meal clean.

The call to train for godliness belongs to the long work of forming a holy people. God made humanity to bear His image, and the training of Timothy is one small piece of that restoring. The discipline is not a ladder to heaven but a response to grace, as Titus 2:11 to 12 says, where the grace of God teaches us to say no to ungodliness and to live self-controlled lives.

The passage looks ahead to the new creation. Paul's promise for 'the present life and the one to come' sets this life's godliness inside the larger hope. In the end the table is not abolished but fulfilled: the Lamb's marriage supper, Revelation 19:9, and the tree of life on both sides of the river, Revelation 22:2. The creation that Paul defended against the ascetics is the creation that God will renew, and the bodies that were trained here will be raised.

quiz.q: How does Paul answer those who forbid marriage and certain foods?

options.text: Every creation of God is good and is to be received with thanksgiving.
options.note: Verses 4 and 5 affirm the goodness of what God made.

options.text: Such rules make Christians holier than others.
options.note: Paul treats these prohibitions as demonic teaching, not a path to holiness.

options.text: Food and marriage are matters of no importance.
options.note: They are good gifts to be received with thanks, not trivial.

options.text: The physical world is inherently evil.
options.note: Paul says the opposite: everything God made is good.

quiz.q: What does Paul urge Timothy to train himself for?

options.text: Godliness, which is valuable for this life and the next.
options.note: Verses 7 and 8 contrast godliness with mere physical exercise.

options.text: Physical fitness above all else.
options.note: Bodily exercise has limited value; godliness is valuable in every way.

options.text: Winning popularity with the crowds.
options.note: The goal is godliness, not popularity.

options.text: Mastering the silly myths of the false teachers.
options.note: Paul tells him to reject those myths entirely.

quiz.q: How is Timothy to handle being young in a place of leadership?

options.text: By setting an example in speech, conduct, love, faith, and purity.
options.note: Verse 12 tells him to be an example so no one despises his youth.

options.text: By hiding until he is older.
options.note: Paul calls him to lead by example now, not to withdraw.

options.text: By ruling harshly to prove himself.
options.note: The call is to godly example, not heavy-handedness.

options.text: By abandoning his gift as premature.
options.note: He is told not to neglect the gift but to use it.

quiz.q: What is Timothy to do with the gift given to him?

options.text: Not neglect it, but be diligent and absorbed in exercising it.
options.note: Verses 14 and 15 urge active use of the gift.

options.text: Keep it hidden so as not to seem proud.
options.note: The danger named is neglect, not overuse.

options.text: Trade it for a more impressive gift.
options.note: He is to use the gift he was given, not exchange it.

options.text: Assume it will grow on its own without effort.
options.note: Gifts unexercised grow cold; Paul urges diligence.

quiz.q: What does Paul say results from watching one's life and doctrine closely?

options.text: By persevering, Timothy will save both himself and those who hear him.
options.note: Verse 16 links perseverance in life and teaching to salvation.

options.text: He will earn salvation by his own effort.
options.note: Salvation is by grace; God saves through faithful means, not by earning.

options.text: Only his hearers benefit, never himself.
options.note: Paul says both himself and his hearers.

options.text: Careful attention makes no real difference.
options.note: Paul insists it is the path God uses to save.

questions: Paul says every good gift is to be received with thanksgiving. Where might you be either despising God's good gifts or grasping them without thanks?
Godliness, like fitness, is trained, not wished into being. What deliberate habits are you building to grow in godliness this season?
Timothy was to be an example despite his youth. In which area, speech, conduct, love, faith, or purity, is your example most needed right now?
Paul warns against neglecting the gift within. What has God gifted you to do that you have been letting go cold, and how will you stir it up?
Watch your life and your doctrine, Paul says. Which of the two, how you live or what you believe, are you more tempted to neglect, and why?

translationNotes.note: The BSB footnote records the variant and suffer reproach for and strive, reflecting differences among manuscript families.
Train yourself renders gymnazo, athletic training language, picturing godliness as strenuous, disciplined exercise, not passive drift.
Save both yourself and your hearers speaks of God saving through faithful, persevering ministry; it does not make the minister the author of salvation.
